title: The Last Winter of the Snow Painter
summary: Every winter is painted into being by a single old artist in a tower at the top of the world. Now he is going blind, and must teach a successor before the last of his sight fails — but Perla learns that the snow was never painted with the eyes, and that the master has been afraid of the wrong loss all along.

chapters.title: The Tower Where Winter Is Made
chapters.body:
Nobody in the lowlands knew that winter had to be painted. They thought it simply came, the way rain comes, or night. But high at the top of the world, on a peak above all the peaks, there stood a slender tower of blue-white stone, and in that tower lived an old man whose task was to paint the winter into being, every year, for the whole world below.

His name — or the name the mountain-folk gave him, for no one knew his real one — was the Snow Painter. And his work was this: through the long dark autumn, he stood at a great window at the top of his tower, before a canvas as wide as the sky, and he painted. He painted the first frost that would silver the low valleys, and the shape of every snowflake, and the way the light would fall blue across the drifts, and the particular grey of a winter sky heavy with coming snow. And as he painted each thing, it became real in the world below — the frost he brushed onto his canvas crept across the lowland fields, the snow he painted fell from the lowland skies. Winter was his painting, made real. Without him, the world would have no winter at all — only an endless, exhausted, unresting autumn, the trees never sleeping, the earth never resting under its white blanket, the year never turning.

He had painted the winter for longer than anyone could count. And now he was going blind.

It had come on slowly, the way it does — a blurring at the edges, a dimming of the light, colors going grey and then gone. He had hidden it for as long as he could. But now the darkness had crept in so far that he could barely see his own canvas, and he was terrified, because he believed that when the last of his sight failed, he would no longer be able to paint the winter, and the world below would be left with no winter forever — no rest, no turning, no white silence, only the endless grinding autumn. So he had sent word down the mountain, at last, that he needed an apprentice. Someone with young, clear eyes, to learn his craft and take up the brush before his own sight failed entirely.

Perla was fourteen, a mountain-girl with sharp eyes and a steady hand, and she was the one the village sent up. She climbed for three days through the deepening cold, and arrived at the blue-white tower half-frozen and full of wonder, and the old Snow Painter received her with a desperate, trembling hope.

"You can see," he said, gripping her hands, his own eyes clouded and searching. "Tell me you can see. Clearly. Every color. Every edge."

"I can see," said Perla, gently.

"Then there's time," the old man breathed, echoing a thing he must have said to himself a thousand frightened times. "There's still time. I'll teach you to paint the winter before my eyes go dark. Quickly. We must be quick. Before I can't show you anymore."

chapters.title: The Lesson That Wouldn't Take
chapters.body:
The old Snow Painter tried, through the long darkening autumn, to teach Perla to paint the winter. And it did not work, and his terror grew.

He taught her what he could see to teach — the technique of it. How to grind the blue-white pigments, how to hold the great brushes, how to mix the exact grey of a snow-sky and the exact silver of first frost. Perla learned it all quickly; she had a good eye and a steady hand, and soon she could copy the old man's strokes so well you could hardly tell them apart. But when she painted frost onto the great canvas, no frost crept across the lowland fields. When she painted snow, no snow fell. Her paintings were beautiful, and perfectly accurate, and completely dead. They were only pictures. They did not become real.

The old man could not understand it, and his failing eyes and failing time made him frantic. "You're doing it exactly as I do," he said, peering blindly at where he knew her canvas hung. "The color is right — tell me the color is right —"

"The color is right," Perla said. "It's exactly like yours. But nothing happens."

"Then you must be seeing it wrong," he said desperately. "There must be some detail your eyes are missing. Look harder. Look closer. It's in the seeing — it must be in the seeing —" And he drove her to look ever more closely, to copy ever more exactly, certain that the magic lived in the precision of the sight, and that if only Perla could see keenly enough, her painting would come alive as his did.

But the winters would not come from Perla's brush, however keenly she looked. And the old man's sight dimmed further with each passing week, and his panic became despair. "When I can't see at all," he whispered one night, huddled by the fire, "the winter will end. Not just for me. For the world. Forever. Because I never managed to teach you, and it's my fault, I left it too late, I was too proud to admit my eyes were failing until it was almost gone —" He wept, the dry weeping of the very old and very frightened. "I have painted the winter all my life, and I am going to be the one who lets it die, because I cannot make you see what I see."

Perla sat with him through that despair, and she thought. And because she was not frozen by the old man's terror — because she could look at the problem from outside it — she began to notice something he, in his panic, had missed.

She had been watching the old man paint, on the days his sight still allowed it. And she had noticed that he did not really look at his canvas as he worked. His clouded eyes drifted, unfocused; he painted the snow not by looking, but by some other sense entirely — his hand moving as if it remembered, as if he were listening to something, or feeling it, rather than seeing it. The frost he painted came alive not on the days his sight was clearest, but on the days his heart was fullest — when he spoke, as he worked, of the winters of his childhood, of the hush of snow, of the way the cold felt and the way the white silence made him feel. On those days the magic flowed. On the days he only copied what winter looked like, precisely and coldly, nothing came alive at all — even when his eyes were at their best.

And Perla began to suspect that the old man had been afraid of the wrong loss all along. That the winter had never been painted with the eyes at all.

chapters.title: What the Snow Was Painted With
chapters.body:
On the night the last of the old man's sight finally failed — when the world went fully dark before his clouded eyes, and he sat trembling, certain he had just doomed the winter forever — Perla took his hands and told him what she had come to understand.

"You've been afraid of the wrong thing," she said gently. "All this time, you thought the winter came from your eyes. That the magic was in seeing clearly, and that when you went blind, you'd lose the power to paint it. That's why you drove me to look harder and harder, and why it never worked — because you were teaching me the wrong sense. The winter was never painted with your eyes, master. I've watched you. It was painted with your heart."

The old man went still.

"On the days your painting came alive," Perla said, "you weren't looking at all — your eyes were already half-gone. You were remembering. Feeling. You painted the hush of snow because you loved the hush of snow, and knew in your body how it felt to stand in it. You painted the blue winter light because it moved you. The magic was never in copying what winter looks like. It was in loving what winter is. That's why my paintings stayed dead, however perfectly I copied yours — I was painting the picture of a winter, from the outside, with only my eyes. You were painting the feeling of it, from the inside, with everything you are. And that, you can do blind. In fact —" she hesitated, then said it — "I think you may do it better blind. Because now nothing distracts you. Now there's only the feeling left."

The old man's blind eyes filled. "But I'm afraid," he whispered. "I've leaned on my sight so long. If I take up the brush now, in the dark, and nothing comes — if the winter doesn't answer —"

"Then we'll find out together," said Perla. "But I don't think you'll fail. I think you've been painting from your heart all along, and just believed it was your eyes. Come. Autumn has gone on too long down below. The world is tired. Let's make it winter."

And she led the blind old man to the great window, and put a brush in his hand, and guided it to the canvas he could no longer see. And she said, "Don't paint what snow looks like. You can't, now, and it never mattered anyway. Paint what it feels like. Tell me about the best winter of your whole life, and paint that."

And the old man, standing blind before the canvas as wide as the sky, began — haltingly at first — to speak of a winter from his boyhood, before the tower, before the burden: a morning he woke to the whole world gone white and silent, and ran out into it laughing, and lay down in the deep snow and felt the huge hushed peace of it, and was, for one perfect hour, purely and simply happy. And as he spoke, he painted — not with his eyes, which were dark, but with his hand and his memory and his whole full heart. He painted the feeling of that white morning. The hush. The peace. The cold clean joy.

And far below, in the exhausted lowlands, the first snow of winter began to fall.

Perla watched it through the window — the frost racing across the distant fields, the snow-clouds gathering grey and heavy, the white blanket settling at last over a world that had waited too long for its rest. The winter had come. The old man, blind as stone, had painted it truer and more beautiful than he had in years — because for the first time in a long time he was not carefully copying what winter looked like, but pouring out what it felt like to love it.

He wept, when Perla told him the snow was falling. But this time it was not the dry weeping of terror. It was something else — relief, and wonder, and a grief for all the years he'd spent afraid of losing a thing he'd never needed.

"All this time," he murmured. "All this time I thought the light was the gift. And it was only ever the loving."

Perla stayed with him after that, and she did learn to paint the winter — but not the way he'd first tried to teach her. She learned it the true way: not by copying what winter looks like, but by going out into the cold and the white and the hush until she loved it in her bones, until she knew in her own heart the peace and the ache and the clean joy of it, and could paint that feeling from the inside. Her first true winter came alive on the canvas not because her eyes were sharp, but because her heart was full. And the old man, blind and content, stood beside her as she painted, and could tell — by some sense far deeper than sight — the exact moment her snow began, at last, to fall.

He painted a few more winters, in the dark, each one truer than the last. And when at last he laid down the brush for good, he was not afraid, because he knew the winter was in good hands — hands that had learned the real secret. And Perla painted the winter for the world for the rest of her long life, and taught it, in time, to a successor of her own. And the first thing she taught, always, before the pigments or the brushes or any of the craft, was this: that the snow is not painted with the eyes. It never was. It is painted with the heart — and so it is a thing you can give the world even in the dark, even at the very end, as long as there is love left in you for the cold white beautiful hush of it. And there always is. There always is.
